aldemar.standfirst: Trump rejected Tehran’s proposal on Saturday — terms that asked the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days — and Iran said it would not soften its demands. Alex Karp said AI needs reasonable guidelines and suggested the frontier labs be nationalised to shield them from liability, because every single one of my clients is going to sue. That is the thesis stated plainly.
UBS raised its target to $250 from $220 after AIPCon; DA Davidson is also at $250 and Rosenblatt at $225.
P/E 148, forward P/E 91 on revenue up 78.9% over the trailing year. The multiple is the risk; the growth is why it is tolerated.

markets.title: Gold drops 3.5% — its biggest move in months, and the story of the session
markets.note: Gold did something it is not supposed to do. Its 3.52% fall was 2.41σ, the largest reading on this board since crude's collapse a week ago — and it happened on the day a Middle East peace proposal was rejected and oil rose 4.22%. WTI's move was 1.25σ, the S&P's 0.77% fall 1.13σ and the Nasdaq's 0.92% 1.01σ. When bullion sells off into an escalation, the marginal buyer is not thinking about geopolitics at all — it is looking at a 5.2% ten-year, a 19-year high, and deciding that a non-yielding asset costs too much to hold.

changed.title: Gold sold off into a war escalation, which tells you what is really setting prices
changed.note: 1. A 2.4 sigma fall in gold on the day a peace proposal collapsed is the most informative thing on the board. Trump rejected Iran's offer, oil rose 4.22%, Brent reached $108.50 — and bullion fell 3.52%. The textbook says gold rises on geopolitical risk. It did the opposite because the ten-year is at 5.2%, a 19-year high, and the cost of holding an asset that yields nothing has gone up faster than the risk premium. This is the third time in two weeks gold has fallen through an escalation. The pattern is now established, and it says the curve is the only variable that matters.

weekly.headline: The week crude gave back the war premium — and the ten-year made four straight highs anyway
weekly.standfirst: Crude fell 7.8% across the week, from $100.70 to $92.89, after Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for an easing of military pressure — an 8.6% single-session collapse on Tuesday — before missiles were fired at Yanbu, the terminal Aramco’s pipeline bypass routes to. The equity week belonged to technology: the Nasdaq rose 2.06% and the S&P 1.21%, both driven by a two-sigma Monday in which Meta’s Muse agent revived the CPU-demand trade. Underneath it, the ten-year went to 5.225%, its highest since 2007, making fresh highs on four consecutive sessions, and the five-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007 — on a PMI at a five-year high rather than on inflation. In the book nothing was opened, closed or moved: OKTA rose 7.06% across the week despite giving back two thirds of its Oktane gain on a Friday sector downgrade, PLTR rose 6.77% and completed its recovery, and AAPL closed at its best mark. Every position is green. Heat 3.00R against 3.0R, unchanged all week and unchanged for a fortnight.

sections.html:
Sigma (σ) measures a move against that instrument’s own recent behaviour, not against zero. Here it is measured on weekly changes over the last twenty weeks, so one sigma is an ordinary week and two is a week bigger than roughly 95% of the last twenty.

Crude fell 7.8% across the week, from $100.70 to $92.89, by way of $89.42 on Tuesday and a rebound to the mid-nineties on Thursday. At 0.98 sigma it led the board, though only just — crude has been this volatile for a month, so a 7.8% week is now close to ordinary for it. Nothing on the board cleared two sigma on a weekly basis.

The equity week belonged to technology. The Nasdaq rose 2.06% to 27,068.72, the S&P 1.21% to 7,743.41, the Dow 0.28% and the Russell fell 0.38%. Monday did most of it: a 2.43 sigma Nasdaq session and a 2.27 sigma S&P session, on Meta's Muse agent reviving the CPU-demand trade — Intel +12.17%, AMD +9.95% and past a trillion dollars, Arm double digits, Meta itself +11.34%. That was one week after an essay from Anthropic's Dario Amodei asked AI companies to slow down.

The curve is the story that did not stop. The ten-year went from 4.94% to 5.225% across the week, its highest since 2007, making fresh 52-week highs on four consecutive sessions. The five-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007 on Wednesday and held it. The trigger was not oil and not inflation: a PMI showing business activity at a five-year high. Growth data raising the discount rate is the version of this problem that cheaper energy cannot offset.

And equities rose into it anyway. The S&P was flat on Thursday and up 0.51% on Friday while the long end made new highs both days. Either earnings can carry a five-percent curve or the market has not marked it yet; there is no data to settle that until 28 October. Gold fell 1.91% across the week as the geopolitical premium came out, and bitcoin held above $84,000.

A week with no decisions in it, and every position finished green

PLTRSoftware: infrastructure · entered 2026-08-27 at 184.45 · stop 164.45 · 13.30% away+0.26R+6.77%+2.83% etd
AAPLConsumer electronics · entered 2026-08-28 at 321.96 · stop 301.99 · 11.46% away+0.96R+1.47%+5.94% etd
OKTASoftware: identity & security · entered 2026-09-14 at 182.73 · stop 162.61 · 16.69% away+0.62R+7.06%+6.82% etd

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Heat is 3.00R against a 3.0R cap, exactly where it was a week ago and a fortnight ago, because heat is set by entries, stops and sizes and none of those changed. No position came within nine percent of its stop at any point in the five sessions. After a fortnight that cost this book three positions, a week of doing nothing is the result, not the absence of one.

The two AI-governance holdings led the week and gave part of it back in the last two sessions. OKTA rose 7.06% across the week and PLTR rose 6.77% — the two best performers in either book. Both peaks came on Wednesday and Thursday; Friday's sector downgrade took OKTA from +1.19R back to +0.62R in a single session. AAPL gained 1.47% and closed the week at its best mark since entry.

OKTA's round trip is the week's lesson about event trades. It went into Oktane at 196.62, reached 212.50 intraday on Thursday, and closed Friday at 195.19 — below where it started the event. The company did everything it could have: a consortium with eight of the largest names in enterprise computing, the only generally-available product in its category, a 25-37.5% pricing uplift. Bernstein downgraded the whole sector two days later on valuation. A good investor day is not a catalyst if the sector re-rates around it.

PLTR completed the recovery this week. It closed above its 184.45 entry on Tuesday for the first time, reached 192.59 on Thursday, and finished at 189.67 — +0.26R, against −0.94R and 0.75% of stop clearance on 10 September. Two weeks ago this was the position most likely to go; it is now 13.30% clear of its stop and up 6.77% on the week. The ten cents that spared this stop when the other account's went are worth about $5.22 a share so far.

The AI trade split in two, and the rate channel switched from oil to growth

1. Selling AI governance and paying for AI capacity are now separate trades. On Wednesday Okta launched a consortium to secure AI agents and rose 4.46%; Palantir, which sells the control layer, rose 3.68%; Alphabet raised 2026 capex to $195-205bn and fell 3.58% — all in the same session. For ten days this brief tracked those three names as one AI-narrative exposure. That framing is now wrong and the better one is simpler: the market is paying for the toll booth and charging for the road. It matters because the two halves can be held separately, and because they will re-couple on any day the whole theme is repriced.

2. The rate channel changed underneath all of it. For a week, falling crude pulled the curve down and let long-duration technology run. Then Wednesday's PMI showed business activity at a five-year high, the five-year Treasury cleared 5% for the first time since 2007, and the ten-year made fresh highs on four consecutive sessions to 5.225%. Good growth is now the rate risk, and cheaper oil cannot offset it. Every position in this book is a long-duration multiple, so this is the single most consequential change of the week — and the equity market's response so far has been to rise.

3. Valuation reasserted itself at the end of the week, in the one place this book is most exposed. Bernstein downgraded Palo Alto, Okta and SentinelOne on Friday because the group had run roughly 100% this year, and Zscaler — named in Okta's own alliance two days earlier — fell 8.64%. Morgan Stanley took the other side, arguing AI-driven security spending justifies the multiples. Both are arguments about price rather than demand, which is the specific risk of owning a re-rated sector: the business can keep improving while the multiple compresses.

Tehran offered to reopen the strait and then missiles were fired at the terminal

Tuesday was the offer. A senior Iranian official said Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports — a proposal delivered through mediators six days earlier. Secretary of State Rubio said the administration was open to that. WTI fell 8.6% to $89.42, a 2.68 sigma session and the largest single reading on this board in a month. A Trump-Pezeshkian meeting was ruled out.

Thursday was the escalation. Iran-aligned Houthi forces fired missiles at Saudi cities including Yanbu and Taif. Yanbu is the Red Sea terminal the East-West pipeline runs to — the endpoint of the entire workaround Aramco has been building since 13 September. Talks stalled at the UN, with Pezeshkian telling the General Assembly Iran would not bend at the knee and an official conceding the sides remained far apart. Crude rebounded 3.9%. A pipeline that can be repaired is a six-week problem; a terminal that can be hit is not.

Friday was the offer again, and crude eased 1.82% to $92.89 on renewed truce discussion under Qatari mediation. Across the week crude fell 7.8%, and it is now $11 below where it traded when twelve of eighteen Fed members projected another hike. Monday's supporting evidence still stands: satellite imagery showed Saudi Arabia moving 2.8m barrels a day through Hormuz against 700,000 in August. But the price now moves on statements rather than barrels, and a negotiation is not a trend.

Wednesday closes the quarter. Expect rebalancing and window-dressing flow through Tuesday and Wednesday — movement without information. Every position in this book had a strong quarter, so any month-end reallocation runs against them rather than with them. It is noise, and nothing here is within nine percent of a stop, so it is noise that can be ignored.

Then the calendar is empty for five weeks. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple on the 29th, Palantir on 2 November, Okta in early December. No company event on any holding before then, followed by three earnings reports and a rate decision inside four sessions. A month of nothing and then everything at once.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the cybersecurity de-rating extends past one Bernstein note — OKTA carries a 16.7% cushion, so it is a question about gain rather than capital. Whether the ten-year keeps making highs while equities rise, which is the clearest measure of complacency available. And whether Yanbu is struck again, which would turn the oil story back from a negotiation into a supply problem and put the Fed's projected hike back on firm ground.

The standing discipline. Heat is at the cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable regardless of what it returns. Every holding is green, the nearest stop is comfortably distant, and there is no catalyst to trade for a month. This week the right decision was made five times by not being made at all.

Crude fell 7.8% across the week, from $100.70 to $92.89, by way of $89.42 on Tuesday and a rebound to the mid-nineties on Thursday. At 0.98 sigma it led the board, though only just — crude has been this volatile for a month, so a 7.8% week is now close to ordinary for it. Nothing on the board cleared two sigma on a weekly basis.

The equity week belonged to technology. The Nasdaq rose 2.06% to 27,068.72, the S&P 1.21% to 7,743.41, the Dow 0.28% and the Russell fell 0.38%. Monday did most of it: a 2.43 sigma Nasdaq session and a 2.27 sigma S&P session, on Meta's Muse agent reviving the CPU-demand trade — Intel +12.17%, AMD +9.95% and past a trillion dollars, Arm double digits, Meta itself +11.34%. That was one week after an essay from Anthropic's Dario Amodei asked AI companies to slow down.

The curve is the story that did not stop. The ten-year went from 4.94% to 5.225% across the week, its highest since 2007, making fresh 52-week highs on four consecutive sessions. The five-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007 on Wednesday and held it. The trigger was not oil and not inflation: a PMI showing business activity at a five-year high. Growth data raising the discount rate is the version of this problem that cheaper energy cannot offset.

And equities rose into it anyway. The S&P was flat on Thursday and up 0.51% on Friday while the long end made new highs both days. Either earnings can carry a five-percent curve or the market has not marked it yet; there is no data to settle that until 28 October. Gold fell 1.91% across the week as the geopolitical premium came out, and bitcoin held above $84,000.

A week with no decisions in it, and every position finished green

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position), exactly where it was a week ago and a fortnight ago, because heat is set by entries, stops and sizes and none of those changed. No position came within nine percent of its stop at any point in the five sessions. After a fortnight that cost this book three positions, a week of doing nothing is the result, not the absence of one.

The two AI-governance holdings led the week and gave part of it back in the last two sessions. OKTA rose 7.06% across the week and GOOG fell 0.97%. Both peaks came on Wednesday and Thursday; Friday's sector downgrade took OKTA from +1.19R back to +0.62R in a single session. AAPL gained 1.47% and closed the week at its best mark since entry.

OKTA's round trip is the week's lesson about event trades. It went into Oktane at 196.62, reached 212.50 intraday on Thursday, and closed Friday at 195.19 — below where it started the event. The company did everything it could have: a consortium with eight of the largest names in enterprise computing, the only generally-available product in its category, a 25-37.5% pricing uplift. Bernstein downgraded the whole sector two days later on valuation. A good investor day is not a catalyst if the sector re-rates around it.

GOOG had the week's only real thesis development, and it was not good. Alphabet raised 2026 capital spending to $195-205bn in the same week OpenAI cut GPT-6 API prices by roughly half and Anthropic shipped Opus 5.5 about 40% cheaper. The stock fell 3.58% on Wednesday and took the position from +1.07R to +0.45R before recovering to +0.75R by Friday. The stop question raised when it crossed +1R on Monday remains open. The underlying issue is now concrete: $200bn of spending discounted at 5.2%, producing something whose price is falling 40-50% a year.

The AI trade split in two, and the rate channel switched from oil to growth

1. Selling AI governance and paying for AI capacity are now separate trades. On Wednesday Okta launched a consortium to secure AI agents and rose 4.46%; Palantir, which sells the control layer, rose 3.68%; Alphabet raised 2026 capex to $195-205bn and fell 3.58% — all in the same session. For ten days this brief tracked those three names as one AI-narrative exposure. That framing is now wrong and the better one is simpler: the market is paying for the toll booth and charging for the road. It matters because the two halves can be held separately, and because they will re-couple on any day the whole theme is repriced.

2. The rate channel changed underneath all of it. For a week, falling crude pulled the curve down and let long-duration technology run. Then Wednesday's PMI showed business activity at a five-year high, the five-year Treasury cleared 5% for the first time since 2007, and the ten-year made fresh highs on four consecutive sessions to 5.225%. Good growth is now the rate risk, and cheaper oil cannot offset it. Every position in this book is a long-duration multiple, so this is the single most consequential change of the week — and the equity market's response so far has been to rise.

3. Valuation reasserted itself at the end of the week, in the one place this book is most exposed. Bernstein downgraded Palo Alto, Okta and SentinelOne on Friday because the group had run roughly 100% this year, and Zscaler — named in Okta's own alliance two days earlier — fell 8.64%. Morgan Stanley took the other side, arguing AI-driven security spending justifies the multiples. Both are arguments about price rather than demand, which is the specific risk of owning a re-rated sector: the business can keep improving while the multiple compresses.

Tehran offered to reopen the strait and then missiles were fired at the terminal

Tuesday was the offer. A senior Iranian official said Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports — a proposal delivered through mediators six days earlier. Secretary of State Rubio said the administration was open to that. WTI fell 8.6% to $89.42, a 2.68 sigma session and the largest single reading on this board in a month. A Trump-Pezeshkian meeting was ruled out.

Thursday was the escalation. Iran-aligned Houthi forces fired missiles at Saudi cities including Yanbu and Taif. Yanbu is the Red Sea terminal the East-West pipeline runs to — the endpoint of the entire workaround Aramco has been building since 13 September. Talks stalled at the UN, with Pezeshkian telling the General Assembly Iran would not bend at the knee and an official conceding the sides remained far apart. Crude rebounded 3.9%. A pipeline that can be repaired is a six-week problem; a terminal that can be hit is not.

Friday was the offer again, and crude eased 1.82% to $92.89 on renewed truce discussion under Qatari mediation. Across the week crude fell 7.8%, and it is now $11 below where it traded when twelve of eighteen Fed members projected another hike. Monday's supporting evidence still stands: satellite imagery showed Saudi Arabia moving 2.8m barrels a day through Hormuz against 700,000 in August. But the price now moves on statements rather than barrels, and a negotiation is not a trend.

Wednesday closes the quarter. Expect rebalancing and window-dressing flow through Tuesday and Wednesday — movement without information. Every position in this book had a strong quarter, so any month-end reallocation runs against them rather than with them. It is noise, and nothing here is within nine percent of a stop, so it is noise that can be ignored.

Then the calendar is empty for five weeks. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple on the 29th, Palantir on 2 November, Okta in early December. No company event on any holding before then, followed by three earnings reports and a rate decision inside four sessions. A month of nothing and then everything at once.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the cybersecurity de-rating extends past one Bernstein note — OKTA carries a 16.7% cushion, so it is a question about gain rather than capital. Whether the ten-year keeps making highs while equities rise, which is the clearest measure of complacency available. And whether Yanbu is struck again, which would turn the oil story back from a negotiation into a supply problem and put the Fed's projected hike back on firm ground.

The standing discipline. Heat is at the cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable regardless of what it returns. Every holding is green, the nearest stop is comfortably distant, and there is no catalyst to trade for a month. This week the right decision was made five times by not being made at all.
